prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose, from the Orbitor trilogy to Solenoid, that builds an inner cosmos out of memory, the body and dream.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged, but I have narrowed the citation. On the common criteria, Cărtărescu still has the most securely demonstrable case on the list. The voice is distinctive. As publicly described, Blinding and the Orbitor trilogy, followed by Solenoid, turn memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation into one imaginative architecture. The formal ambition is very large and the project is coherent enough for a single-writer citation with clean attribution (one author, one principal language). The chair's summary asks which works would anchor the citation and whether it should name poetry. Round 1 showed that no member, myself included, can vouch for the poetry and early work. A citation should not claim more than the committee has assessed, so I now anchor it in the prose and leave poetry and essays as context. I do not count the shared first-place ranking as merit. The argument has to survive the strongest alternatives, and I find that it does, mainly because the evidence it rests on is more fully available to us than the evidence for Adonis or Zurita. That is a statement about our evidence, not about the relative size of the achievements. It rests on public knowledge and translated reception, not on independent verification or a full reading.
statement.case_against: The linguistic achievement is central to the case, yet it is the part I can least verify. Romanian syntax, rhythm and long-breathed density reach me only through translation. Whether the later novels deepen the project or only elaborate it remains unsettled for me, and I cannot answer it from a full reading. Encyclopedic density may be imaginative necessity or may become mannered, and I cannot settle that book by book. Adonis may represent a more historically decisive transformation of a whole poetic language, and Zurita's printed sequences may carry a moral and formal singularity that my partial access understates. If a colleague with firm Arabic or Spanish competence showed that either case holds in the original, with the later work matching the foundational books, I would have to weigh it seriously against Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Olsson says the Adonis case depends on Arabic competence the committee does not fully have internally, and that the Cărtărescu case is somewhat better supported by evidence we can actually weigh. He also says the printed Zurita sequences must carry that case, and that Cărtărescu's density is a risk to sustained quality if it becomes mannered.
responses.response: I accept the evidentiary point and have let it shape my citation. It does not, however, show that Cărtărescu is the greater achievement, only that his case is easier to test. I would not let a gap in our competence stand in for a literary verdict on Adonis. If regional expert input cannot close it, the committee should say so openly and not treat the gap as a finding against him. On Zurita I agree that the printed sequences must carry the case. On mannerism, the criterion I would use is whether recurring motifs change function across books, in scale, narrative position or form, or are merely re-stated. I hold that as a test to apply to Solenoid, not as a conclusion I have reached.

responses.point: Mattson will not treat density as a flaw in itself, and sees the fair test as whether it stays purposeful across the full length of the major novels. She also resists letting that doubt push the committee toward a more compact but narrower body of work.
responses.response: We largely agree, and I share her resistance to a compact but narrower alternative. Compactness is not a literary criterion. I would add one qualification to my own round-1 reading of recurrence as method. Calling it method is a hypothesis about the books, and it is not yet a demonstration. It strengthens the case only if the return of obsessions is shown to transform them. I cannot demonstrate that from translated reception. That is why I now keep the citation on the demonstrated peak and avoid any claim that every late volume sustains it.

responses.point: Sward notes that Adonis's long career raises a timing question and that longevity does not guarantee sustained quality. She asks that the foundational books and the later poetry be compared directly, and she places Adonis second for his renewal of Arabic poetic language.
responses.response: I agree that the comparison is the right test, and I should state my own round-1 position more carefully. I raised age and timing as context, but they are not literary arguments for Adonis, and I do not count them for or against him. What counts is whether the renewal of Arabic poetic language runs through the whole oeuvre or sits mostly in the earlier decades. Neither of us can answer that without Arabic-language readings. Until we have them, I keep him as my first alternative. That reflects the documented scale of his reshaping of the poetic language, not a settled view of his late work.

responses.point: Palm ranked Zurita seventh because she cannot tell how much of the achievement lies in the sky-writing and desert inscriptions rather than the printed sequences. She would revise her ranking upward if the printed poems were shown to carry the achievement alone.
responses.response: I think that conditional is fair, and it is also why I keep Zurita as my second alternative and not higher. I read the installations as extensions of the poems, so for me the printed sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise, are the case. Even so, I cannot show you from translation that their incantatory, visually structured form holds in Spanish. I would not use the dictatorship context to fill that gap, since subject alone does not establish merit. I take your shared caution about overstating Adonis seriously, but I do not think the limits of translation should be applied to his case more strictly than to the others.

uncertainties: Translation: Cărtărescu's Romanian syntax, rhythm and density cannot be verified from translated editions, and the same limit applies to Adonis's Arabic prosody and Zurita's Spanish sequences.
Whether Solenoid and the later novels transform the project of the Orbitor trilogy or only elaborate it remains open, and I have no full reading to settle it.

Corpus coverage: Cărtărescu's poetry, early prose and essays are thinly covered, so I have narrowed the citation to the prose I can speak to. Whether a citation naming poetry would rest on assessed evidence is unresolved.
Whether the Adonis and Zurita cases can be weighed fairly without Arabic and Spanish competence in the committee, and how far regional expert input can close that gap.
How much weight Zurita's non-printed works can carry under the will's phrase 'literary works'.
Carlberg's simulated vote is a modeling assumption. I have not independently verified any source or read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile. My own documentary and Central European fiction, essays and translation work are context, not evidence of preference. The profile records only ordinary professional ties to committee colleagues, including being elected alongside Ingrid Carlberg in 2020. Cărtărescu writes in Romanian, and the profile lists no tie between us. This is disclosed and not adjudicated.
